items.title: Top K Frequent Elements: count karo, phir frequency ke buckets
items.one_idea: Top K Frequent Elements: count every value with a hash map, then use the count itself as a bucket index so the top k come out in O(n) without sorting.
items.spoken_hook: Top K Frequent Elements: sorting के बिना O(n) में!

items.visual_idea: The array row [1,1,1,2,2,3,4,4,4,4] feeds a count table (value: count); then a row of buckets indexed 1 to 10 where each value drops into the bucket numbered by its count, and a pointer walks the buckets from 10 down to 1, collecting values until k=2 are picked; beside it a sort-everything bar of about 17n steps shrinks against the bucket bar of about 2n.
items.everyday_anchor: none: the owner's rule (2026-10-26) is technical register for working engineers with no everyday analogies; the idea is explained by the count table and bucket index only.
items.example: EXAMPLE nums=[1,1,1,2,2,3,4,4,4,4], k=2: counts {1:3, 2:2, 3:1, 4:4}; buckets[4]=[4], buckets[3]=[1], buckets[2]=[2], buckets[1]=[3]; walking from 10 down gives [4, 1]. Also [1,1,1,2,2,3] k=2 gives [1, 2]; [1] k=1 gives [1]. For n=100000 (EXAMPLE) sorting all counts ~1700000 steps (n log2 n) versus ~200000 for count plus bucket pass.
approach_order: problem: return the k most frequent values, answer unique, any order
brute force: count each value by rescanning the array for every element, O(n^2), or count once and sort all (value,count) pairs, O(n log n) which the follow-up forbids
bottleneck: sorting orders all distinct values though only the top k are needed
optimization 1: min heap of size k, O(n log k) (Counter.most_common(k) does this)
optimization 2: a count can only be 1..n, so use count as a bucket index: buckets[c] = values with count c; walk c from n down to 1 until k values are collected, O(n) time
complexity: time O(n), extra space O(n) for the counter and n+1 buckets
facts_to_verify: Problem paraphrased from the doocs mirror of LeetCode 347 (leetcode.com returned 403 this session): k most frequent elements, answer unique and any order, 1 <= n <= 10^5, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4, follow-up asks for better than O(n log n). Builder re-checks against the problem page if reachable.

Hash table + min heap of size k is O(n log k) time, O(k) heap space per the doocs page; the same page says Counter.most_common(k) does this heap selection. The Python Counter docs fetched do NOT state its complexity: do not claim it from the docs, cite doocs only.

Bucket approach O(n) time and O(n) extra space is the planner's own analysis (counts lie in 1..n, one pass to count, one pass over n+1 buckets plus the distinct values); the doocs page gives no bucket solution and Wikipedia's bucket sort gives O(n) average only for k~n buckets. Label as derived, never as a quoted source. Say 'extra space O(n)', counter and buckets.

The exact displayed Python was run this session: output Counter({4: 4, 1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1}), topK([1,1,1,2,2,3,4,4,4,4],2) = [4, 1], topK([1],1) = [1], topK([5,5,6,6,6,7],2) = [6, 5], and 5000 seeded-free random arrays (values -5..5, n<=30) matched the sorted top-k count multiset. Builder reruns it and shows the real output on screen.
Tie caveat: the problem guarantees a unique answer, so ties at the k boundary never occur; the code's tie order is arbitrary and the reel must not claim an order among equal counts.

Heapq docs: nlargest/nsmallest perform best for small n, sorted() is better for larger n; heappush/heappop big-O is not stated in the docs (only 'logarithmic' in the Theory section) so do not quote log k for push from the docs.
Step counts 1700000 vs 200000 for n=100000 are EXAMPLE arithmetic (n*17 vs 2n), not measured timings.
